doc.title: Vince Giordano interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

title: Hardships of the road in the old days
summary: Musicians then faced bad conditions, food and southern racism, yet shared camaraderie.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: It’s interesting to speculate. Because I sometimes feel like I was born too late. Maybe not too late as you might have been born too late, but I was into the swing era a great deal. I wonder what it would have been like to live through that.

Um hum. Well it was rough. Talking to all these musicians and reading their stories of fellows I didn’t get a chance to meet, the fellows talked about their life on the road and the horrible conditions, the terrible food. I mean today musicians have it easy, you know, they really do. They don’t have the work but they have it easy. © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
That’s a great statement. When they do get the work it’s easier.

Oh yeah. I mean they’ve got an air conditioned place or a heated place, the piano is basically in tune if it’s not they’ll bring in an electric keyboard or whatever. The accommodations, the buses, and not to speak of all the horrendous racial stuff that went on in the south with black musicians. It was just awful. I don’t know how guys did it. And it makes me even more appreciative of what these musicians did with all those hardships.
The fellows that I’ve been able to talk to from that era just have an awful lot of love for one another. Somehow the music sustained them, made all that stuff, you know they dealt with it somehow.
Yeah. There was this camaraderie, they were all in it together.
